item.title: [International Logistics #3] Buses vs. Taxis on the Ocean: How the Shipping Market Really Works
item.body:
> Ocean shipping splits into two markets, scheduled "liner" service and on-demand "tramp" service. Carrier alliances share ships, and freight indexes track what it costs to move goods.

## Today's Concept

About 80% of world trade by volume travels by sea, but "shipping" isn't one market. It's really two, and they run on different rules.

**1. Liner shipping: the ocean bus.**
Liner carriers run fixed routes on published schedules. A ship leaves Shanghai every week whether it's full or not, and it calls at the same ports in the same order. Liners mostly carry **containers** of manufactured goods like electronics, clothing, furniture, and auto parts. Thousands of shippers share each vessel, much like passengers on a bus. Small shippers usually pay rates quoted by the carrier or a freight forwarder. Large shippers negotiate annual **service contracts**.

**2. Tramp shipping: the ocean taxi.**
Tramp ships have no fixed schedule. They go wherever a cargo owner needs them to go. They mainly carry **bulk** commodities such as iron ore, coal, grain, and crude oil, often filling the whole ship with a single cargo. The deal is called a **charter**, and there are three main types:
- **Voyage charter**: you pay to move one cargo from port A to port B.
- **Time charter**: you rent the ship and its crew for a set period.
- **Bareboat charter**: you rent only the ship and supply your own crew and operations.

**Shipping alliances.**
A modern container ship can carry more than 20,000 containers, and running a weekly service needs several of them. To fill that much space, carriers form **alliances**. Members share space on each other's vessels through vessel-sharing agreements, which lets them offer more routes and sailings than any one of them could run alone. Alliances share *ships*, but they don't set *prices* together; each carrier still sets its own rates. That makes them different from the older **liner conferences**, which did fix prices. The EU banned conferences in 2008. In the US, carrier agreements are filed with and overseen by the Federal Maritime Commission (FMC).

As of 2025, the main groupings were the **Gemini Cooperation** (Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd), the **Ocean Alliance** (CMA CGM, COSCO/OOCL, and Evergreen), and the **Premier Alliance** (ONE, HMM, and Yang Ming). **MSC**, the world's largest container line, operates on its own. Alliance membership changes every few years, so check current lineups before relying on them.

**Freight indexes.**
Shipping prices swing widely, so the industry tracks them with indexes:
- **Baltic Dry Index (BDI)**: published by London's Baltic Exchange. It tracks the cost of chartering dry bulk ships and is often read as a signal of raw-material demand.
- **Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI)**: spot container rates for routes out of Shanghai.
- **Drewry World Container Index (WCI)** and **Freightos Baltic Index (FBX)**: spot container rates on major east-west routes, usually quoted per 40-foot container (FEU).

## In Everyday Life

Picture a mid-sized furniture importer in Dallas that buys sofas from a factory near Shanghai. Its goods travel by **liner**: containers ship weekly to the Port of Los Angeles/Long Beach, then go by rail to Texas. The importer has an annual service contract with one carrier, plus a forwarder to book extra space on the spot market during busy months.

In 2021, demand surged during the pandemic and ports backed up. Spot rates from China to the US West Coast, measured by indexes like the FBX, climbed above **$20,000 per 40-foot container**. Before the pandemic they had typically been under $2,000. Importers who relied on the spot market saw shipping costs jump, which pushed up retail prices. Importers with contracts were better protected, though not always, because some carriers struggled to honor every contracted slot.

Meanwhile, a grain exporter in New Orleans shipping soybeans to Asia uses the **tramp** market. It charters a whole bulk carrier, and it watches the **Baltic Dry Index** rather than container indexes.

Same ocean, different markets.

## 3-Line Summary

1. **Liner** shipping runs fixed, scheduled routes for containerized goods (the bus). **Tramp** shipping is chartered on demand for bulk cargo (the taxi).
2. **Alliances** let container carriers share vessel space to offer wider networks, but unlike old conferences, they don't fix prices.
3. **Freight indexes** like the BDI (bulk) and SCFI, WCI, and FBX (containers) track volatile shipping costs that directly affect product prices.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** A steel mill rents a bulk carrier and its crew for 12 months to move iron ore wherever it needs. What kind of arrangement is this?
- A) Liner service contract
- B) Voyage charter
- C) Time charter
- D) Bareboat charter

**Q2. (True/False)** Members of a modern container shipping alliance jointly set the freight rates they charge customers.

**Q3.** Which index would you watch to track the cost of chartering ships that carry coal and grain?
- A) Shanghai Containerized Freight Index
- B) Baltic Dry Index
- C) Freightos Baltic Index
- D) Drewry World Container Index

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Liner shipping**: Scheduled ocean service on fixed routes, mainly for containers, open to many shippers.
- **Tramp shipping**: Unscheduled ocean service in which ships are chartered to carry cargo, usually bulk, wherever it's needed.
- **Charter party**: The contract for hiring a ship (voyage, time, or bareboat).
- **Shipping alliance**: A group of container carriers that share vessel space and coordinate services without fixing prices.
- **FEU (Forty-foot Equivalent Unit)**: A standard 40-foot container, the usual unit for quoting container freight rates.

---

*Answers: Q1 – C. Renting a ship with its crew for a set period is a time charter. A voyage charter covers a single trip, and a bareboat charter excludes the crew. Q2 – False. Alliances share vessel space and schedules, but each carrier sets its own prices. Joint price-fixing was the feature of the old liner conferences. Q3 – B. The Baltic Dry Index tracks dry bulk charter costs. The other three track container rates.*
